HIGHWAY ROCK THROWING

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We investigate the motives behind this scourge of rock throwing incidents across South Africa – are we dealing with a spree of dangerous pranks or a wicked plan to rob motorists?

Unique Selling Point:
CURRENT ON THE NEWS CIRCUIT - OF NATIONAL INTEREST

NOT BEING REPORTED HOW WIDESPREAD THE PROBLEM IS IN GAUTENG - CURRENTLY MOST MEDIA COVERAGE IS IN KZN WHERE THE ISSUE IS NOT NEARLY AS BAD AS IT IS IN GAUTENG

Summary:
The spotlight has been case on rock throwing incidents recent weeks – having claimed two siblings lives in KZN, with seven subsequent attacks.

But the issue is not limited KZN – in fact, it’s much worse in Gauteng.

There have been at least 39 incidents reported in Gauteng since 2016 – having claimed 5 lives to date, caused a number of injuries, thousands of rands worth of damage to vehicles and in many cases resulted in robberies of the motorists.

We look at the motives behind this senseless crime and ask what the authorities are doing.


Further information:
KZN CASE STUDY - THE DEATH OF SIBLINGS
On December 28, Amina Haffajee, 16, and her brother Abdur Raheem, 7, were killed after a boulder thrown from a bridge crashed through the windscreen of their vehicle on the N2 highway near Tongaat in KwaZulu-Natal.

It has been reported that the rock ripped through the windshield and hit Haffejee. The force at which it landed caused her seat to fly back‚ hitting her brother. (the family are from Gauteng – they were on holiday in KZN)

Since then there have been at least 10 (7 in KZN & 3 in GP) more highway rock throwing incidents.

GAUTENG CASE STUDY – SAFFIYA KAROLIA
I, myself lost my beloved father on the 14 September 2016 tragically when his car struck one of the rocks on the n12 resulting in a fatal accident. I therefore feel very strongly about this issue and surely someone has to be held accountable for the safety of people when they are aware of this problem yet very little is being done to prevent it and it continues to happen everyday.

THE MOTIVE
Highway rock-throwing is causing havoc on South African roads terrorising road-users.

It could be a wreckless prank or a wicked plan by thieves to rob motorists. In many of the Gauteng cases motorists are robbed of their belongings when they are forced to stop after. The irony is that the damaged caused to the vehicles is usually way more than the value of the goods stolen from the car.

There is no clear pattern – cases take place at night and even in broad daylight.

WHAT ARE AUTHORITIES DOING
If you ask the community in Lenasia, Gauteng – they will tell you not enough. They have been campaigning for the last two years to get authorities to act. But they have had to take up the cause themselves and have groups that patrol the hotspots, remove rocks and warn motorists of potential threats.

In KZN, the metro police have deployed blue light patrols at the hotspots – but they admit this isn’t a long term solution. They have set up a provincial joint task team under Department of Transport and Community Safety. A R250 000 reward has also been put out for any information related to these incidents.

SANRAL
It’s SANRAL responsibility to keep our roads safe. Although most new bridges are enclosed with a type of caging – many older bridge are still open. In 2012 there was talk of night vision camera’s to be installed after a spurt of attacks in KZN (not sure if it was actually done)

HOW DO WE TELL IT
We use KZN as a springboard to tell the bigger story of rock throwing across South Africa and particularly in Gauteng.

VISUALS
- I have pictures of the damage and rocks on the roads.
- I have one GREAT video of an actual rock throwing on a dash cam.
- Then I have drone footage of the N12 hotspots.
- I will get visuals of the KZN bridges and the sight where the Haffejees were killed.

INTERVIEWS
- THE HAFFEJEE FAMILY (hopefully the parents, but probably a spokesperson) – they are based in Gauteng and were on holiday on KZN when their children got killed.
- SAFFIYA KAROLIA – her father was killed in a rock throwing incident in 2016.
- The Lenasia Crime Info Group – Mohammed Bulbulia – he will explain the extent of the highway rock throwing and the community’s pro-active involvement.
- SANRAL – what are they doing?
- MEC for Community Safety in Gauteng // the Police // JMPD

Press Release:


Highway Rock Throwing
It’s a deadly practice, often with fatal consequences. Gauteng and KZN have seen a renewed spate of rock throwing from highway bridges, causing serious damage to vehicles, claiming lives and injuring several motorists. But are these just reckless pranks or part of a devious plan to rob injured motorists of their valuables


Script:


ROCK THROWING STRUCTURE

VO: The spotlight has been cast on Rock Attacks this past festive season. Two siblings, Amina Haffejee and Abdur Raheem, were killed on the N2 outside of Durban - after a rock was thrown off a bridge - smashing into the car they were travelling in.

LINK: It’s a senseless crime – causing panic and claiming lives on our road across. The motives are debatable – are we dealing with a dangerous pranks or devious plans to rob unsuspecting motorists.

VO: While the Haffejee family grieves their loss, they are still too traumatised to speak. Since then, there have been at least 7 rock-throwing incidents in the Durban area.

ALIZIA: It sounded like a gun shot actually went off – and I saw my passenger window was broken – I got the fright of my life
KIRTHAN: it was quite a loud noise, // I saw the crack on the screen and I said oh shucks this is what happened.

VO: Durban Metro Police’s Deputy Head of Operations Sbonelo Mchunu says it’s not a new trend.

MCHUNU: But it’s new in KZN in this magnitude. It happened in 2016, galvanised our resources // and it died down. It has just resurfaced now.

VO: Aliza Cilliers was travelling to Durban from Westbrook Beach on the North Coast two weeks ago, around 9 AM. As she passed through a tollgate on the N2, she noticed people on the side of the road, moments before her car was pummelled with rocks.

ALIZIA: It took me a few seconds to actually realised what happened, lucky it wasn’t the windscreen, otherwise I would have pulled over.

VO: Kirthan Pillay’s incident happened a week ago, when he drove under the Boy’s Town Bridge on the M4 just outside of Durban. He has no doubt in his mind that it was a rock-throwing incident.

KIRTHAN: It couldn’t have been a stone from the road because it was quite big and quite high on the windscreen.

VO: Durban Metro’s Mchunu says it’s difficult to know the true motives, as the culprits have yet to be brought to book.

MCHUNU: There have been some suspects have been arrested and investigated – but no convictions yet.

ALIZA: It’s scary, it’s scary to be on the road and to think that someone can throw something from any bridge, that someone can throw something from the side of the road.

LINK: And it’s not limited to KZN – the malicious act of throwing rocks from freeway bridges plagues motors across the country.

VO: In Gauteng, while there have been rock throwing attacks as recent as last week, it seems the modus operandi has shifted to placing rocks on the road surface to cause obstruction.

Just two days after the fatal Haffejee incident in KZN - Luis Antoinio was driving with his brother-in-law Riaan Viviers on the N17 towards Johannesburg just before sunrise.

Luis: Went through the tollgate and next thing there was a rock in the way – I had nowhere to go, I hit the rock full on - from there it was just a disaster.

VO: The vehicle rolled and came to a halt under the next bridge – Luis says the rocks weren’t thrown at the car, but were all over the road making it impossible to avoid them.

LUIS: I almost lost my life, brother in law almost lost his life, I mean my daughter just got in high school.

VO: Saffiya Karolia’s father was, not, so lucky.

SAFFIYA: Our family has been so severely impacted by this – we’ve lost my dad // we miss him every day – every single day

VO: Saffiya and her brother, Shaheen took us to the scene of the accident. Their father hit rocks on the N12 in September 2016 in the early hours of the morning.

BROTHER: There were four rocks placed here on the road – one was placed here on the right, one on the left, again on the right and then again the left lane. My father tried to avoiding the one rock and then hit the next rock.

VO: Ebrahim Karolia died on the scene.

While there haven’t been any other fatalities in Gauteng, there has been at least 30 other incidents along that stretch of road since 2016.

SAFFIYA: After my father’s passing I joined the N12 group- felt needed to proactive – couldn’t sit back – lets do something – let be proactive about it.

VO: The community group patrols the area, keeping a watch out for potential threats and regularly has clean up operations, removing rocks from the side road that could be used in attacks.

Mohamed Bulbulia took us to one of the affected bridges. The most recent attack was on Christmas day when a car’s sunroof was hit as it went under the bridge.

BULBULIA: At times the rocks are placed on this side of the railing and they push it over // because the rocks are big it’s not going to fall directly – it could fall in either lanes.

VO: But it’s not easy to see the perpetrators from a distance says Mohamed.

BULBULIA: For instance we are standing – we might look like ordinary citizens but we might be the criminals as well. If you look by the time you come here – it’s too late for you to change because sometimes there is a vehicle in the other lane//.

LINK: These reckless acts go beyond the scope of the traffic police, while they can patrol the roads and be more visible – we’re not dealing with straight forward traffic violations – this is criminality that should be investigated by the South African Police Service.

VO: Brigadier Vish Naidoo says these attacks are a serious concern for the police.

VISH: We have a situation that is called displacement of crime – when we start to police those areas – criminals move on they start to find other areas where they could find victims to be more vulnerable //as long as people are hungry they will commit crime// people are committing crime to make a buck.

VO: In June 2017, Muhammad Adam became a victim of this crime, when he and a friend, drove along the N12 in Jo’burg one night.

MUHAMMAD: I was in the right lane, I was in this lane – I saw the rock in the middle of the lane

VO: He couldn’t change lanes, and drove over the rock, damaging the car. But when Muhammad got out to assess the situation, he was approached by a group of men almost immediately – he quickly got back into the car.

MUHAMMAD: They asked if needed help // insisted tried opening the door // pointed the gun at me and broke the window with same gun.

VO: They were robbed of all their belongings and the guys made off into the darkness.

MUHAMMAD: I am still very scared to use this road – I would suggest that anyone use the road before the sunsets.

BULBULIA: It’s a provincial road, lighting stops at national road so when it’s dark there is opportuners there that are taking advantage of the situation.

LINK: This particular stretch of road vulnerable to rock incidents – if look at the area next to the freeway you’ll see there are communities on both sides of the road – making it easier for culprits to throw a rock, to disappear without a trace.

VO: The challenges are similar in KZN says Durban Metro’s Mchunu.

MCHUNU: We’ve been having those problems in securing proper evidence. // this needs community participation – community people will know who are the rogues who do these things.

SAFFIYA: it’s not only the responsibility of community members to keep that road safe – government needs to step up.

VO: Only National roads are the responsibility of SANRAL - the rest is Provincial government. Vusi Mona from SANRAL, believes rock attacks are indicative of lawlessness.

VUSI: it difficult for SANRAL – we are just engineers, not law enforcers

VO: Brigadier Naidoo, whose job it is to enforce the law says the police have both a pro-active and reactive role to play – but not in isolation.

VISH: The way to prevent it from happening is to ensure high-density visibility from police officers but this cannot be a sustainable initiative – it cannot be there forever. //

VO: While additional SAPS & traffic police patrols have been implemented temporarily, joint tasks teams with the relevant Government role players have been set up in KZN and Gauteng – Saffiya believes infrastructure improvement is the answer.

SAFFIYA: At the very least lighting on that stretch – and should come up with a long-term solution – they have a duty and responsibility to ensure the safety of the road users.

VO: The Gauteng Department of Roads & Transport takes care of provincial infrastructure – MEC Ismail Vadi says, lighting is in the pipeline.

MEC: The COJ has indicated that there is a plan in place for the lighting of the informal settlement – we thought it would be a practical option to wait for.

VO: In KZN, the task team is looking to secure bridges.

MCHUNU: The strategy at the moment is to fence most of the bridges to make it difficult for them to bring big rocks on the bridge.

VO: MEC Vadi is not convinced that it is a viable solution for the N12.

MEC: We are talking about 4 on / off ramps and three bridges. // it’s not just closing up one bridge, have picked up from the community – they feel like being caged up – we don’t want to live in cages.

VO: Another option, is cameras on bridges, but with over 2300 overpass bridges just in the SANRAL road network – Spokesperson Vusi Mona says it comes with a high price tag.

VUSI: There are bridges that have cameras // but someone has to pay for camera – where will it come from – SANRAL? What is the mandate to do cameras or build road? 2300 bridges with cameras – how much is that going to cost.

VO: And while government works on budgets – Luis says people’s lives are at risk .

LUIS: Crime doesn’t sleep – it doesn’t matter what skin colour you are – it doesn’t matter.

SAFFIYA: People are living in fear, it’s a form of terrorism almost. // we are no longer just hijackings and robberies there is the risk of fatalities.


PROMOS

PROMO 1

VO: Gauteng and KZN have seen a renewed spate of rock-throwing crime.

ALIZIA: It sounded like a gun shot actually went off // I got the fright of my life //
VO: Are these reckless pranks or a devious plan to rob motorists?
PROMO 2
VO: We investigate the motives behind a scourge of highway rock-throwing incidents across South Africa, causing panic and claiming lives on our roads.
SAFFIYA: // we are no longer just hijackings and robberies there is the risk of fatalities. INT1 M8

PROMO 3
VO: It’s a deadly practice with fatal consequences.

SAFFIYA: We’ve lost my dad // we miss him every day – every single day INT1 M9

VO: What’s behind the spate of rock-throwing incidents from highway bridges across Gauteng and KZN?

VISH: We have a situation that is called displacement of crime – when we start to police those areas – criminals move on they start to find other areas where they could find victims to be more vulnerable //as long as people are hungry they will commit crime// people are committing crime to make a buck. VO: In June 2017, Muhammad Adam became a victim of this crime, when he and a friend, drove along the N12 in Jo’burg one night. MUHAMMAD: I was in the right lane, I was in this lane – I saw the rock in the middle of the lane VO: He couldn’t change lanes, and drove over the rock, damaging the car. But when Muhammad got out to assess the situation, he was approached by a group of men almost immediately – he quickly got back into the car. MUHAMMAD: They asked if needed help // insisted tried opening the door // pointed the gun at me and broke the window with same gun. VO: They were robbed of all their belongings and the guys made off into the darkness. MUHAMMAD: I am still very scared to use this road – I would suggest that anyone use the road before the sunsets. BULBULIA: It’s a provincial road, lighting stops at national road so when it’s dark there is opportuners there that are taking advantage of the situation. LINK: This particular stretch of road vulnerable to rock incidents – if look at the area next to the freeway you’ll see there are communities on both sides of the road – making it easier for culprits to throw a rock, to disappear without a trace. VO: The challenges are similar in KZN says Durban Metro’s Mchunu. MCHUNU: We’ve been having those problems in securing proper evidence. // this needs community participation – community people will know who are the rogues who do these things. SAFFIYA: it’s not only the responsibility of community members to keep that road safe – government needs to step up. VO: Only National roads are the responsibility of SANRAL - the rest is Provincial government. Vusi Mona from SANRAL, believes rock attacks are indicative of lawlessness. VUSI: it difficult for SANRAL – we are just engineers, not law enforcers VO: Brigadier Naidoo, whose job it is to enforce the law says the police have both a pro-active and reactive role to play – but not in isolation. VISH: The way to prevent it from happening is to ensure high-density visibility from police officers but this cannot be a sustainable initiative – it cannot be there forever. // VO: While additional SAPS & traffic police patrols have been implemented temporarily, joint tasks teams with the relevant Government role players have been set up in KZN and Gauteng – Saffiya believes infrastructure improvement is the answer. SAFFIYA: At the very least lighting on that stretch – and should come up with a long-term solution – they have a duty and responsibility to ensure the safety of the road users. VO: The Gauteng Department of Roads & Transport takes care of provincial infrastructure – MEC Ismail Vadi says, lighting is in the pipeline. MEC: The COJ has indicated that there is a plan in place for the lighting of the informal settlement – we thought it would be a practical option to wait for. VO: In KZN, the task team is looking to secure bridges. MCHUNU: The strategy at the moment is to fence most of the bridges to make it difficult for them to bring big rocks on the bridge. VO: MEC Vadi is not convinced that it is a viable solution for the N12. MEC: We are talking about 4 on / off ramps and three bridges. // it’s not just closing up one bridge, have picked up from the community – they feel like being caged up – we don’t want to live in cages. VO: Another option, is cameras on bridges, but with over 2300 overpass bridges just in the SANRAL road network – Spokesperson Vusi Mona says it comes with a high price tag. VUSI: There are bridges that have cameras // but someone has to pay for camera – where will it come from – SANRAL? What is the mandate to do cameras or build road? 2300 bridges with cameras – how much is that going to cost. VO: And while government works on budgets – Luis says people’s lives are at risk . LUIS: Crime doesn’t sleep – it doesn’t matter what skin colour you are – it doesn’t matter. SAFFIYA: People are living in fear, it’s a form of terrorism almost. // we are no longer just hijackings and robberies there is the risk of fatalities. PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: Gauteng and KZN have seen a renewed spate of rock-throwing crime. ALIZIA: It sounded like a gun shot actually went off // I got the fright of my life // VO: Are these reckless pranks or a devious plan to rob motorists? PROMO 2 VO: We investigate the motives behind a scourge of highway rock-throwing incidents across South Africa, causing panic and claiming lives on our roads. SAFFIYA: // we are no longer just hijackings and robberies there is the risk of fatalities. INT1 M8 PROMO 3 VO: It’s a deadly practice with fatal consequences. SAFFIYA: We’ve lost my dad // we miss him every day – every single day INT1 M9 VO: What’s behind the spate of rock-throwing incidents from highway bridges across Gauteng and KZN? metadata.Summary: The spotlight has been case on rock throwing incidents recent weeks – having claimed two siblings lives in KZN, with seven subsequent attacks. But the issue is not limited KZN – in fact, it’s much worse in Gauteng. There have been at least 39 incidents reported in Gauteng since 2016 – having claimed 5 lives to date, caused a number of injuries, thousands of rands worth of damage to vehicles and in many cases resulted in robberies of the motorists. We look at the motives behind this senseless crime and ask what the authorities are doing.
metadata.Further information: KZN CASE STUDY - THE DEATH OF SIBLINGS On December 28, Amina Haffajee, 16, and her brother Abdur Raheem, 7, were killed after a boulder thrown from a bridge crashed through the windscreen of their vehicle on the N2 highway near Tongaat in KwaZulu-Natal. It has been reported that the rock ripped through the windshield and hit Haffejee. The force at which it landed caused her seat to fly back‚ hitting her brother. (the family are from Gauteng – they were on holiday in KZN) Since then there have been at least 10 (7 in KZN & 3 in GP) more highway rock throwing incidents. GAUTENG CASE STUDY – SAFFIYA KAROLIA I, myself lost my beloved father on the 14 September 2016 tragically when his car struck one of the rocks on the n12 resulting in a fatal accident. I therefore feel very strongly about this issue and surely someone has to be held accountable for the safety of people when they are aware of this problem yet very little is being done to prevent it and it continues to happen everyday. THE MOTIVE Highway rock-throwing is causing havoc on South African roads terrorising road-users. It could be a wreckless prank or a wicked plan by thieves to rob motorists. In many of the Gauteng cases motorists are robbed of their belongings when they are forced to stop after. The irony is that the damaged caused to the vehicles is usually way more than the value of the goods stolen from the car. There is no clear pattern – cases take place at night and even in broad daylight. WHAT ARE AUTHORITIES DOING If you ask the community in Lenasia, Gauteng – they will tell you not enough. They have been campaigning for the last two years to get authorities to act. But they have had to take up the cause themselves and have groups that patrol the hotspots, remove rocks and warn motorists of potential threats. In KZN, the metro police have deployed blue light patrols at the hotspots – but they admit this isn’t a long term solution. They have set up a provincial joint task team under Department of Transport and Community Safety. A R250 000 reward has also been put out for any information related to these incidents. SANRAL It’s SANRAL responsibility to keep our roads safe. Although most new bridges are enclosed with a type of caging – many older bridge are still open. In 2012 there was talk of night vision camera’s to be installed after a spurt of attacks in KZN (not sure if it was actually done) HOW DO WE TELL IT We use KZN as a springboard to tell the bigger story of rock throwing across South Africa and particularly in Gauteng. VISUALS - I have pictures of the damage and rocks on the roads. - I have one GREAT video of an actual rock throwing on a dash cam. - Then I have drone footage of the N12 hotspots. - I will get visuals of the KZN bridges and the sight where the Haffejees were killed. INTERVIEWS - THE HAFFEJEE FAMILY (hopefully the parents, but probably a spokesperson) – they are based in Gauteng and were on holiday on KZN when their children got killed. - SAFFIYA KAROLIA – her father was killed in a rock throwing incident in 2016. - The Lenasia Crime Info Group – Mohammed Bulbulia – he will explain the extent of the highway rock throwing and the community’s pro-active involvement. - SANRAL – what are they doing? - MEC for Community Safety in Gauteng // the Police // JMPD
